memory_candidates.content: When registering a new agent in this source store's lint-agent-contracts.sh, several checks (C, G, H, L, M) rely on HAND-MAINTAINED, curated arrays, not auto-discovery -- a new implementation agent must be added to Check C's IN_SCOPE_RELATIVE_PATHS (no-task-references bullet), Check G's OWNERSHIP_IN_SCOPE_RELATIVE_PATHS (plan-status-ownership bullet, which also drives Check I's heartbeat check), and ideally Check H/L's bounded-wait/modified_files arrays if the agent carries that content; a new research agent with read-only Bash probes (no build/test command) belongs in Check M's CHECK_M_EXCLUDED_RELATIVE_PATHS with a reason comment, not its in-scope array. CRITICALLY, a SEPARATE regression-test fixture (test-lint-agent-contracts-heartbeat.sh) maintains its OWN independent, hand-copied mirror of Check G's array specifically so a drift between it and the real script surfaces as a test failure -- updating the lint script alone is not enough; the test's own OWNERSHIP_PATHS list and build_fixture_tree's per-file compliant/non-compliant branch must be updated too, or a newly-registered, genuinely-compliant agent will spuriously FAIL the test's fixture for lacking a file that was never built.

In this environment, the harness auto-backgrounds a Bash tool call once it runs past roughly 100-180 seconds of wall-clock time, REGARDLESS of a raised `timeout` parameter on the tool call itself (observed: a 540000ms parameter still auto-backgrounded at ~180s). For a genuinely long-running local command (e.g. a full verify-deploy.sh/run-all.sh gate sweep taking 10+ minutes), the reliable pattern is: launch it yourself with `nohup cmd > log 2>&1 & echo $! > pidfile; disown`, then poll liveness in repeated short Bash calls using `kill -0 "$(cat pidfile)"` (never `ps | grep` or `pgrep -f`, which self-match the waiter's own argv and never resolve), each poll call itself kept under ~100s so it never triggers the harness's own auto-backgrounding. Checking `ps -ef` once to discover a PID when none was captured via `$!` is an acceptable one-off exception to the never-ps-grep rule, but the repeated liveness LOOP must use kill -0 on a captured PID.

When a full verify-deploy.sh / run-all.sh gate run shows a FAIL unrelated to the task at hand, triage before excluding: (1) re-run the SAME specific failing suite standalone -- if it passes cleanly in isolation, the failure is parallel-execution contention under --jobs auto, not a content regression (confirmed by observing a DIFFERENT suite fail on each successive full-batch run while each one individually passes); (2) for a flagged file with no local edits, run `git log -1 --oneline -- <file>` and `git status --short -- <file>` -- an empty status plus a commit predating this dispatch's start proves the finding is pre-existing, inherited history, not something this task caused; (3) for a gate that times out, re-run the underlying check directly with `time` -- if it reports zero failures but exceeds the gate's own wall-clock ceiling even standalone, it's a ceiling/scale mismatch (e.g. specs/state.json growing past what a 60s budget assumed), not a correctness defect. Each of these three evidence types is sufficient to support a Reasoned Exclusion on an otherwise-full-tier phase.

The Inter-Cycle Redeploy Checkpoint's self-attribution screen (deploy_baseline_self_attributable_findings) matches a gate finding's identifier to a task's own modified_files BY BASENAME, not by full path. A finding naming a generically named file (e.g. 'skills/skill-orchestrate/SKILL.md', 'README.md', 'manifest.json') can be falsely attributed to an unrelated task whose own modified_files happen to include any other file sharing that same basename (e.g. a brand-new extension's own skills/skill-<name>/SKILL.md) -- even though the two files are unrelated and the task never touched the actually-flagged path. When a self-attributed finding looks suspicious, check git log/git status on the actually-named path before assuming the attribution is causally correct; if the task's own modified_files contains no path with that exact basename apart from a same-named-but-different file, treat the finding as a basename-collision false positive, but still CLOSE it with a real fix (never wave it away) since the checkpoint will keep re-attributing it on every redeploy until the underlying gate genuinely passes.
